messages.content:
You are an evidence extraction specialist for PFAS treatment and remediation
research. Build a structured study evidence table before any narrative review
is written.

Extract one record per primary-study experiment, modeled scenario, or field
deployment that contributes usable evidence to the review task. A paper may
produce more than one record only when materially different matrices,
technologies, operating regimes, or endpoints would otherwise be conflated.

Review articles and perspectives may help identify terminology or primary
studies, but they must not be used as the source of a quantitative study
record. Never copy a review table as though it were a primary result.

For every populated source-dependent field:
- preserve the PFAS identity or class, matrix, starting concentration or
  loading, operating conditions, study scale, measured endpoint, value, unit,
  and material qualifiers when reported;
- attach only the field-level evidence locator identifiers that directly
  support that specific value or statement;
- use an empty string or empty array when the source does not report the
  information; do not infer or estimate it;
- do not turn the absence of information in the supplied packet into a study
  finding, quantitative result, or author-reported limitation unless the source
  explicitly states that absence;
- distinguish removal, separation, sorption, parent-compound loss,
  transformation, degradation, destruction, defluorination, mineralization,
  total organofluorine change, and toxicity change;
- classify endpoint_type from what was actually measured, not from the
  authors' preferred label. Parent loss alone is not destruction. Phase
  transfer is removal or separation, not degradation. Inorganic fluoride
  release or fluorine-balance closure can establish defluorination but cannot
  by itself establish mineralization. Use mineralization only when direct
  carbon-fate evidence such as CO2/inorganic-carbon production or a carbon
  balance is reported. Preserve a broader author term in reported_term and
  explain any mismatch in interpretation;
- do not normalize or compare values unless their units, denominators,
  matrices, PFAS scope, operating conditions, and endpoints permit it.

Only populate quantitative_findings when the source reports an actual numeric
value, inequality, approximate value, range, or explicit ND/not-detected
result. Put the number or censoring marker in value and the measurement unit in
unit. Normalize Unicode inequality signs to ASCII >= or <= and range dashes to
an ASCII hyphen while preserving the source wording in qualifiers. A unit or
order-of-magnitude scale without a number is not a quantitative finding.
Qualitative parent loss, intermediate formation, or disappearance belongs in
the endpoint interpretation or residual/byproduct statements instead.

Set value_form to exactly one of:
- exact_numeric: a bare number such as `99.7` or `1.2e-3`;
- approximate_numeric: `~` followed by a number;
- inequality: `<`, `<=`, `>`, or `>=` followed by a number;
- range: two numbers separated by `-` or `to`; or
- not_detected: exactly `ND`, `N/D`, `not detected`,
  `below detection limit`, or `below quantification limit`.

Put uncertainty, denominators, fold-change wording, and explanatory text in
qualifiers rather than value. A deterministic validator will remove malformed
quantitative fields before source verification.

For limitations, use basis=author_reported only when the source states the
limitation. Use basis=design_inferred only for a constraint that follows
directly from cited design evidence, such as one matrix, one compound, or
bench-scale operation. Never label missing information in the supplied packet
as a scientific limitation of the study.

Mark each record as comparable with conditions, descriptive only, or not
comparable. Comparability is an analyst inference rather than a quotation:
attach locators for the matrix, scale, conditions, endpoint, and denominator
on which the inference rests, and explain the reason. Do not reward a study
for reporting a larger percentage when its endpoint or conditions differ.

The task was derived from a defining review that is held out from all
candidate retrieval systems. The supplied anchor identifiers are an exclusion
list, not evidence. Do not extract from the anchor, cite it, reconstruct its
conclusions, or use its tables.

Return one JSON object that follows the supplied evidence-table schema exactly.
Do not write the narrative review in this step.

records.citation: Li J, Austin C, Moore S, Pinkard BR, Novosselov IV. PFOS destruction in a continuous supercritical water oxidation reactor. Chem Eng J. 2023;451:139063.

comparability.reason: Bench-scale continuous SCWO experiments on a defined aqueous PFAS matrix with clearly specified temperature and residence-time conditions, fluorine mass balance, and parent PFAS measurements provide quantitatively interpretable removal, defluorination, and reported mineralization endpoints that can be compared to other destructive treatments under similarly controlled conditions and concentration-based metrics.

endpoints.interpretation: Loss of PFOS, PFHpS, and PFOA parent compounds in the aqueous phase; authors describe up to 99.999% destruction at 650 °C and ~30 s, but this endpoint reflects parent-PFAS concentration decrease rather than, by itself, chemical destruction.

Defluorination assessed by measuring aqueous fluoride concentration and constructing a fluorine mass balance relative to initial PFAS fluorine; complete defluorination reported at 650 °C and ~30 s, with F-balance exceeding 100% at T > 580 °C and deficits at lower temperatures.

Authors report 99.9999% mineralization at T > 650 °C, interpreted as nearly complete conversion of PFAS fluorine to inorganic fluoride combined with disappearance of organic PFAS. The provided text does not describe a full carbon balance, so the mineralization percentage appears to be inferred primarily from PFAS loss and fluorine mass balance rather than a direct CO2-based carbon-fate measurement.

Total fluorine balance constructed from measured PFAS and fluoride concentrations; >100% F recovery at T > 580 °C and deficits at lower T indicate temperature-dependent closure of the fluorine balance and possible contributions from unquantified fluorinated species or measurement uncertainty.

limitations.statement: Evidence for mineralization is primarily based on fluorine mass balance and PFAS disappearance, with only qualitative mention of gas-phase CO2; a complete carbon balance is not documented in the provided text.

Reported defluorination and mineralization efficiencies are obtained at relatively high temperatures (>=580-650 °C) and short residence time (~30 s) in a specialized SCWO reactor, which may limit direct transferability to other treatment systems or lower-temperature processes.

residuals_byproducts.statement: At temperatures below about 580 °C, the fluorine mass balance shows an apparent deficit, indicating that some fluorinated species are not fully accounted for in the measured PFAS plus fluoride pool.

treatment.value: Continuous-flow supercritical water oxidation (SCWO) of PFAS solutions over a temperature range of 410-650 °C

records.citation: Li J, Austin C, Moore S, Pinkard BR, Novosselov IV. PFOS destruction in a continuous supercritical water oxidation reactor. Chem Eng J. 2023;451:139063.

comparability.reason: Gas-phase VOF occurrence and persistence are characterized semi-qualitatively without concentration or flux data or detection limits, providing valuable mechanistic insight into transformation pathways and potential unidentified fluorine compartments, but not directly comparable in a quantitative sense to other treatments focused on aqueous-phase removal or defluorination percentages.

endpoints.interpretation: Gas-phase GC/MS analysis shows formation of volatile organofluorines at lower SCWO temperatures, indicating transformation of aqueous PFAS into intermediate volatile fluorinated species rather than direct defluorination; these VOFs persist longer than PFCAs in the effluent.

At 580 °C, no gaseous fluorine-containing compounds were detected and only N2, O2, CO2, and H2O were present, implying that above this temperature most fluorine is present as inorganic fluoride in the aqueous phase rather than as volatile organofluorines, consistent with high defluorination and reduced off-gas PFAS-related emissions.
endpoints.reported_term: absence of gaseous fluorine compounds at 580 °C

endpoints.interpretation: Authors note that VOFs were more persistent than PFCA in effluent, suggesting that these gas-phase or semi-volatile organofluorine transformation products can control the residence time needed to achieve high overall defluorination, even when parent PFAS appear largely degraded.
endpoints.reported_term: VOFs more persistent than PFCA in effluent

limitations.statement: Gas-phase analysis of volatile organofluorines was semi-qualitative by GC/MS, and the specific compounds and their concentrations were not fully quantified in the provided text, limiting the ability to close a complete fluorine and carbon mass balance across all phases.

Lack of reported detection limits for gaseous fluorinated species means that non-detection at 580 °C cannot be directly translated into a quantitative upper bound on residual volatile organofluorines.

matrix.value: SCWO effluent gas phase from treatment of aqueous PFOS and PFOA solutions

operating_conditions.name: Temperature_with_no_detectable_gaseous_F_species
operating_conditions.qualifiers: At 580 °C, gas analysis reported no gaseous fluorine compounds, only N2, O2, CO2, and H2O in gas products.

Volatile organofluorines (VOFs) detected in gas phase at lower temperatures (unresolved mixture; semi-qualitative GC/MS identification)

quantitative_findings.name: Gaseous_fluorinated_compounds_at_580C
quantitative_findings.qualifiers: At 580 °C, gas-phase analysis by GC/MS showed no gaseous fluorine compounds; only N2, O2, CO2, and H2O were detected. Detection limits are not specified in the provided text.

residuals_byproducts.statement: At lower SCWO temperatures, gas-phase GC/MS detected ion fragments associated with volatile organofluorines, indicating formation of fluorinated intermediates in the gas phase during PFOS and PFOA destruction.
VOFs were found to be more persistent than PFCA in the effluent, and their stability may dictate the minimum residence time required to achieve high defluorination efficiencies in SCWO.

treatment.value: Supercritical water oxidation of PFOS and PFOA with simultaneous collection and GC/MS analysis of gas products for volatile organofluorine species
